svg.title: Traditional VPN, ZTNA and SASE compared by access path and trust assumption, with the advantages of ZTNA and the four constraints that slow its migration
svg.desc: Top: three access paths. Traditional VPN takes the endpoint into a gateway and lands it inside the internal network at network-level access, so the trust assumption is that authentication grants a trusted position, and once connected the whole internal network can be scanned. ZTNA takes the endpoint to a broker and then to a specific application at application-level access, trusting nothing and authorising every access separately, so the user never sees internal addressing and cannot scan laterally. SASE routes the endpoint to the nearest point of presence that combines SD-WAN with cloud security, keeping the same never-trust assumption and adding inspection close to the user, which moves security capability into the cloud and merges it with network access. Middle left: the three structural advantages of ZTNA - no network exposure because only applications are published and users get no internal routes; fine-grained permission per application, per identity and per device posture; and auditability because every application access is recorded rather than one tunnel being open for eight hours. Middle right: the four migration constraints - application remediation for non-HTTP protocols such as RDP, SMB and database clients that need connector support; performance because traffic transits a cloud point of presence and latency must be assessed; a hybrid period of two to three years where VPN and ZTNA run in parallel, requiring unified identity and policy; and a cost model change from buying appliances to per-user subscription, which requires recalculating the total cost of ownership. Bottom: a note that the migration is governed by the application inventory, not by the client software, and that the parallel period is where most programmes fail.
svg.text: ZTNA is not a better VPN - it is a different unit of access
A VPN authorises a network position. ZTNA authorises an application session. Everything else follows from that
TRADITIONAL VPN · NETWORK-LEVEL
user
gateway
internal network
every host, reachable
Trust assumption: authenticated means trusted position.
Result: one compromised laptop can scan the whole estate.
Lateral movement is the design, not the accident
ZTNA · APPLICATION-LEVEL
user
broker
app A only
app B, C invisible
Trust assumption: nothing - each access is authorised again.
Result: no internal routes, so scanning has no subject.
Exposure follows the application list, not the subnet
SASE · ZTNA + INSPECTION AT THE EDGE
user
nearest PoP
app / web
SD-WAN + security stack, in one hop
Trust assumption: same as ZTNA, plus inspection
near the user instead of at headquarters.
Result: policy follows the user, not the building.
Cost: latency through a shared PoP, and a vendor exit plan
THREE STRUCTURAL ADVANTAGES OF ZTNA OVER VPN

g.text: Only applications are published, users receive no internal routes,
and scanning has nothing to discover even if the laptop is owned.
Per application, per identity and per device posture - not "logged in",
but "this user, this device state, this application, this session".
Every application access is a record. A VPN gives you one log line:
"a tunnel was open for eight hours" - which answers nothing.

svg.text: FOUR CONSTRAINTS THAT SLOW THE MIGRATION
Application remediation - non-HTTP protocols (RDP, SMB,
database clients, legacy client-server) need connector support
Performance - traffic transits a cloud PoP; measure latency,
and be ready to keep a dedicated path for critical applications
Hybrid period - typically 2-3 years of VPN and ZTNA in
parallel, which requires unified identity and unified policy
Cost model - from buying appliances to per-user subscription,
Migration is governed by the application inventory,
not by the client software: enumerate every application, classify it as web or non-web, and the order of migration writes itself.
Where programmes fail: not in the proof of concept, but in year two, when the VPN still exists for the twelve applications nobody would fund, and two policy systems now disagree.
